c.v: At this point the bench does five things, each proven on a fresh clone outside the working copy, not on a machine that has been lived in.

exits 0 and CI is green on the exact commit cloned. One launch command starts the robot and its world, headless or with the window, with topics matching what we wrote down. The frame tree and the command chain match those drawings too, checked with
rather than by memory. A run recorded with
replays into a fresh monitor, and
and exits 0. And an initial supervisor exists: four fake-input tests pass, and stopping the relay visibly stops the robot.

The decision worth defending is treating a passing row with no proof, or a failing row with no record, as the same problem. Every row gets a written result, and every failure becomes a dated entry in the bench's debugging notes with the command that would find it again, so the milestone stays open until that entry has a fix rather than being quietly forgotten three topics later.
What we can now show: a milestone line in
with today's date, which rows passed the first time, and what is still open, backed by a fresh clone that actually built and ran.

subs.title: Check the milestone list; write the debugging notes so far

c.v: By the end of this session, every item of the milestone list has been run against a fresh clone of the bench, and each one has either passed or has an entry in the bench's debugging notes with a date and a next step.

The five items are the ones everything after them stands on. The scenario runner starts the world, drives the robot through the supervisor, reads odometry back and records what happened, so a weak spot here turns into a day of confusion in three topics' time. Check them on a fresh clone rather than in

items.v: Clone and build. Put the clone outside the workspace you work in, so that nothing of yours leaks into it:

blocks.text:
git clone git@github.com:<you>/test_bench.git /tmp/milestone1
cd /tmp/milestone1
rosdep install --from-paths src --ignore-src -y
./check.sh; echo "exit $?"

c.v: and check three of its versions against the machine you are on now:
. A version that has moved is not a failure, and an undated version list is: add today's date and the new number.

in the clone lists them by name. Then stop the relay in terminal 2 while the robot drives, and watch the supervisor log that odometry is stale and the robot come to a stop. Measuring the stop time from the message stamps was the supervisor topic's job, so here it is enough that it stops and that the number in
still looks like what you see.
Write the result of each row: passed, or failed with one line on what you saw. Anything you can fix in ten minutes, fix now on a branch and merge it. Anything longer becomes an entry in

in the summary step, with today's date and the next step you would take, and the milestone stays open until that entry has a fix. A milestone list with a failed row and no entry is the one outcome to avoid: three topics later, nobody remembers which row it was.

c.v: You are done when every row of the list has a written result, every failure has either a merged fix or a dated entry with a next step, and the fresh clone passes

c.v: Then one entry per problem you met since the environment topic, newest first, each in the same six lines. Here is one from the robot-world topic as the shape to follow:

blocks.text:
## 2026-09-14  The robot doesn't move
Symptom     ros2 topic pub on /cmd_vel ran without an error and the robot stood still.
Seen in     bench_sim world.launch.py, Gazebo Harmonic, nav2_minimal_tb3_sim 1.3.0.
Looked at   ros2 topic info -v /cmd_vel: my publisher offered Twist, the bridge expected TwistStamped.
Cause       the 1.3.0 bridge takes TwistStamped; a publisher of the other type is accepted and ignored.
Fix         publish TwistStamped. The type the installation needs is in docs/simulation.md.
Next time   ros2 topic info -v <topic> before anything else when a message seems to vanish.

c.v: The last line is the one that earns the entry its place, so write it even when it reads as obvious today. An entry without a command that finds the problem again is a diary, and you will not read it twice.
End with two short lists: the tools that found most of these problems, in the order you reached for them, and the questions you now ask before opening an editor. Then add a line to
under the milestone: the date, which rows passed on the first try, and what is still open.
